title: What all share: the jewels
hookLine: every school takes refuge in the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha
tomorrow: What all share: ethics and practice

cards: Buddham saranam gacchami. A room full of people says it together, then again, then a third time.

In a Thai temple at dawn, a Korean mountain monastery, an ordination in a Tibetan hall, a Zen ceremony in a rented room, the words and the tune change, but the shape stays recognizable: three things, named, as places to go for shelter.
Some people describe saying them as the moment they became Buddhist. It's the second thing the schools share.

teach.h: TO THE BUDDHA FOR REFUGE I GO.
teach.b: You met the three jewels on day two, and the refuges on day one twenty-three; today, side by side. First, the words. Buddham saranam gacchami: to the Buddha for refuge I go.
Then the same for the dhamma, the teaching, and the sangha, the community. The old Pali formula then repeats the whole thing a second time, and a third. Second, why refuge.
The Dhammapada pictures frightened people running for shelter to mountains, forests and sacred trees, places that can't really protect them.
Then it names a refuge it calls safe. In Max Müller's translation, it's the one who "takes refuge with Buddha, the Law, and the Church."
Müller's English sounds strange now: Law is his word for dhamma, and Church his word for sangha.
Third, why jewels. Buddhists call the three the triple gem, or the three jewels. Tradition explains the name simply: like gems, they're precious, and worth keeping close.
Fourth, the schools side by side. Theravada communities recite the refuges in Pali, often followed by the precepts.
Zen and other East Asian schools take the refuges in ordination and lay ceremonies, in Chinese, Korean, Japanese or Vietnamese.

In Tibetan Buddhism, refuge prayers are said at the start of practice, and some lineages also name the teacher, the lama, alongside the three. Pure Land and Nichiren communities hold the jewels in their own ways too.

What the Buddha means, what counts as the teaching, who belongs to the community: the schools answer those differently. But across the schools met so far, the three names come back. Tomorrow, the third thing they share.

how: Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, reciting the formula three times in Pali, Chinese, Tibetan, Japanese or another language, at ceremonies, and at the start of practice.

o: the three jewels, Buddha, dhamma and sangha, taken as refuge
the three robes a monk owns: outer, upper and lower
three precious relics kept in the oldest stupas of India

games.q: what all share: tap the pairs.
p: his words for dhamma and sangha

s: the refuge formula is said once
the Pali formula repeats the whole of it a second and a third time.
the Dhammapada calls mountains and sacred trees a safe refuge
it names them as places frightened people run to; it calls the three jewels the safe refuge.
some Tibetan lineages name the lama alongside the three jewels
refuge prayers in those lineages also name the teacher.

games.q: you're frightened, and you look for shelter. the Dhammapada names some places people run to. which does it call safe?
o: the Buddha, the teaching and the community.
games.why: the verses name mountains, forests and sacred trees first, then point to the three jewels as the safe refuge.

practice: Sit upright, palms together if that feels right.

If you're a Buddhist, or wish to be, say the old words slowly, Buddham saranam gacchami, Dhammam saranam gacchami, Sangham saranam gacchami; if they're not your words, simply listen to them in your mind, as words that hold a whole family of schools together.
Then notice, without judging, where you go for shelter when life gets hard: a person, a place, a habit.

wordCard.voice: What all share. The three jewels, the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, in which Buddhists of the schools take refuge. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: to the Buddha for refuge I go. The same line follows for the dhamma and the sangha.

carryVoice: Your line: three jewels for all. Three names that keep on coming back. Until tomorrow.
